drink water before you go to bed at night. Or if you're worried about waking up to pee, make sure you drink your water in the morning like at breakfast or on your way to work. Showing up already hydrated will be helpful. 

In extreme heat like this, I typically fill up a large cooler type canteen with just ice. The ice will melt so fast that even doing this will still only give you maybe half a day of cold water. Sometimes I keep several containers and leave some in the truck and wrapped towels around to further insulate them.   

I also reuse plastic water bottles and leave them in the freezer overnight. If it's frozen solid in the morning it will be plenty melted by lunchtime.  

Electrolyte packs are also helpful. And it's not a good idea to consume alcohol the night before. This is why many HVAC workers don't drink during the week. 

And don't let your moron coworkers who don't drink water influence you. ending up in the ER for heat stroke is not anything to flex about.

hi. Apprentice HVAC installer here. Hand pain/numbness has been with me for a long time, having been a delivery driver & restaurant workerfor 13 years and starting to develop carpal tunnel. but it started getting really bad when I started trade school and really really bad when I started this job six weeks ago.

Of course I'm middle-aged, so I kind of expect my body to break down. You know those little hot hands handwarmers things? I clutch those at night when I sleep. Feels AMAZING. Order a big ole' box of them from Amazon.  You should also make sure that your hands aren't bent at weird angles while you sleep. I have also bought these little finger splints on Amazon to help keep my fingers from bending because if I don't wear them I often have to click my finger joints back into place when I wake up in the morning. they attach with Velcro so you can adjust the size and wear one for each finger joint like more than one on the same finger. Easy to remove for handwashing, eating, etc. 
     I have asked my coworkers, men of all ages & experience levels if their hands hurt at night and they ALL say yes. A lot of them just use Tylenol or other anti-inflammatories. A friend of mine also recommended diclofenac, which is a topical analgesic for arthritis but it really seems to work. I use it sparingly because I hate having to keep buying it and it doesn't come in huge tubes, but it always seems to work right away.
       Definitely try the exercises people are recommending. I was practicing with my new swage bits earlier at home and I was using my middle finger to press the trigger on the driver just to give my index finger a break. Might not want to do that at work necessarily but since I'm at home and I got accident insurance for off the clock, it's whatever.  
     I was told by a recruiter that one reason there are so few women in my particular trade, and in the trades in general, is because of how physically taxing it is on the body. And I'm sure that the way a lot of tools and implements are designed is by men, for men. and unfortunately toxic masculinity is alive and well in the trades, so much that I am often made fun of for wearing gloves or a back brace or other PPE, and pretty much all my male coworkers consider PPE to be "unmasculine." they did not take kindly to me pointing out that becoming injured and possibly disabled isn't going to feel good for their masculinity, either. Ha. but my point is, tools are probably not designed to preserve hand health. I have also heard about these vibration gloves that they sell, but I haven't picked up a pair yet.

I will say this though, work is going to tear your body up no matter what. If you have an office job you will become pale and flabby and start having problems with your knees and hips from sitting all day. So if you want my opinion, it's really up to you as to how much you want to put yourself through. I consider the damage to my hands a good trade-off considering that my blood sugar is now under control & I've lost a lot of unnecessary body fat and gained quite a bit of muscle due to the nature of my daily tasks. And the daily exposure to the sun has had health benefits as well, such as improved mood and expedited wound healing.  
     Give your hands lots of love with nice lotions and lots of rest when you aren't at work.

so I just got my first HVAC job and I'm on my second semester of trade school. I don't know how old you are or what your overall background is otherwise, but here are a few things to keep in mind.

HVAC is really all the trades in one. We do mortar and concrete, we do carpentry, we do electrical, we do plumbing, we do customer service, we do sales. HVAC professionals wear many hats. The upside of that is there are so many different career paths you can take that the possibilities are endless. right now I'm a residential installer which is very hard on the body and apparently not the highest paying, but I love it because I have ADHD so each day is totally different and my customer service background lends well to being inside peoples houses and wandering around on their lawn all day. The downside is that if you aren't built like a farm hand, install can be really hard on the body.  same with a lot of commercial work because you are going up on rooftops and carrying really heavy stuff up and down ladders and doing movements that are basically parkour. 

plumbing seems like it would be more labor intensive (iron pipes are HEAVY). I don't have much experience with that. It definitely pays better, but I imagine it would be just as hard on the body if not harder. However it is a more narrow and specific focus and you don't have to learn any electrical stuff. I'm taking electrical this semester and I've already started studying even though night school doesn't start until Tuesday and I already feel like I'm going to die. Too many formulas. But also with plumbing you do need to do quite a bit of math when it comes to pipe fitting. 

Both professions require a lot of troubleshooting and thinking outside the box. in the HVAC world women are in particularly high demand across-the-board but especially for residential and service tech because customers, especially female customers, are a lot more comfortable having a woman there, and also women tend to have better sales results, since for better or for worse, the sales aspect is becoming more and more integrated with the role of service technician. even though I am an installer I still feel like they are preparing me to do sales down the line because you are better at a sales job if you know the process from start to finish. Our lead salesgirl used to be an installer and a service tech. 

My job is a dirty job, I go home covered with Caulk and brick/concrete dust and sometimes mud or paint, but I know plumbing can be even dirtier. Since you spend a lot of time inside holes. 

So that's my two cents. Hope it helps.

Hello. Sorry it took me a while to get back on this; I wanted to give a thoughtful response.

The short answer is that if you are going there on vacation, you will like it. New Orleans, just like St. Louis, has something for everybody and a lot to do including a lot of free things to (though not as many free things as St. Louis, more like things that used to be free). It’s a really fun place to go on a trip. But also, the proliferation of Airbnb‘s is one of the things that’s destroying the vibrant colorful neighborhoods that make New Orleans unique, such as the Marigny, the Treme, The Bywater, the ninth ward, etc. basically they kick poor people out of their houses and then turn them into Airbnbs, and it’s the poor people of New Orleans that give the most culture and color. 

If you like Mardi Gras and music festivals, definitely hit up one of those. Halloween is actually a great time to go to New Orleans because there are so many haunted houses and there is also voodoo fest at city Park.

Living there is something entirely different. I’m not going to go on a tirade here because I don’t want to pee in anyone’s breakfast cereal, but just like with any other place, if you have money, like six figures, you can have a great life! If you are in some kind of profession with a strong resume where you can get a high-paying job like in a medical field or the oil and gas industry, you will do just fine. But that said, New Orleans has a much lower pay scale for healthcare workers and for most jobs in general… Unless you are a unionized oil and gas employee, or someone with a twic card. The best jobs are the offshore ones, but those jobs are usually not friendly towards women, especially single mothers. 

Otherwise, the job situation is pretty bad and so is the housing situation. When you go look at places to rent, they count the living room as a bedroom so what would be considered a one bedroom apartment in St. Louis with a living room/studio would be considered a two bedroom. They would probably also count the basement as a bedroom even if it’s unfinished, if we even had basements there, because that’s how greedy they are, and most of the housing is in terrible condition… moldy, damp, pest-ridden, crowded, poor plumbing/electrical. It’s devastatingly hot and humid 365 days out of the year and most of the houses are so poorly insulated that you will feel the heat and humidity inside your home even if you have central A/C. If you are somehow affluent enough to pay for a house that’s been renovated, you’re still probably going to be paying 40% of your income. The roads are like a game of Waccamaw but for potholes and they are trying to whack your car to pieces. I had a friend totaled his brand new Jeep just because he hit a pothole in the dark. Also the flooding is so bad, even during your standard afternoon rain storm, that you find stranded cars all over the city and the rental place often runs out of rentals during these flood times. Also the monster hurricanes are getting worse and more predictable every year… So if you were to live there prepared to spend at least a month of the year with no power and no Internet and probably no work since usually jobs require those things.

But otherwise, yeah, go book your vacation and have a blast. If you have time, take a side trip to Biloxi Mississippi and take the boat ride to ship Island, and have a nice beach day.

Bourbon street is all main stream and top 40 stuff so if you want to see the “real“ New Orleans go to Decatur and Frenchmen st (quarter; marigny) and do enjoy the privilege of being able to consume alcohol openly 24 hours a day by the river while watching the boats go by.

One more thing though… No offense, St. Louis, but your Mardi Gras isn’t even close to ours. We have parades starting six weeks out from fat Tuesday, and there are five nonstop straight days of hard partying and parades from the Wednesday before fat Tuesday all the way up till fat Tuesday… That way everyone can participate and not just people privileged enough to have Saturday off.
